implementation_notes: This is the one language where the pattern is a library call in the standard: Proxy.revocable(target, handler) returns the forwarder (proxy) and the revoker (revoke) as a pair, so the grantor keeps revoke and hands out proxy. What replaces the classic structure is exactly that factory - no enable slot, gate or per-method check is written by hand, because every operation on the proxy goes through the handler's traps. After revoke() any trap throws a TypeError, the call is idempotent, and it detaches proxy from both target and handler, so the target becomes collectable while the collaborator still holds the (now useless) proxy; there is no way to re-enable it.
pitfalls: typeof does not trigger a trap, so a revoked proxy still reports 'object' and truthiness, and calls already inside a trap continue to run - the revoked state guards new operations, not work in progress.

revoke() detaches target and handler from the proxy (the proxy lives in a private field of the revoke function, not in a closure), so keeping the revoker alive does not keep the proxy alive, and the target can be collected even while the collaborator still references the proxy.
Calling revoke() again has no effect and never restores access; there is no enable path, so a design that needs re-granting must build a new revocable proxy.
